description_full: BHP Group Limited operates as a resources company in Australia, Europe, China, Japan, India, South Korea, rest of Asia, North America, and South America. The company operates through three segments: Copper, Iron Ore, and Coal. It explores for copper, iron, steelmaking coal, energy coal, nickel, potash, cobalt, sulphide, ammonium sulphate, silver, gold, molybdenum, uranium, and zinc deposits. The company is also involved in the services, marketing, trading, and finance businesses; potash, nickel, and copper development; mining, smelting, refining of nickel; and provision of towing, freight, administrative, and marketing support and other services. BHP Group Limited was founded in 1851 and is headquartered in Melbourne, Australia.

financial_summary: BHP Group Limited is a mega-cap basic materials business with a $202.0B market cap on $51.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -8% over the past three years, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 26% against a 9% cost of capital — a 17-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $9.3B in free cash flow — roughly 18 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.68× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.4× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 11.0×.

Shareholder yield of 4.0% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 19% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Piotroski score 4/9 — below the median for a healthy business
Weakness in commodity prices pressures materials companies
Commodity price volatility and cost-curve position — in a downturn only the lowest-cost producer has a business, and the rest carry the overhead.
Environmental remediation liability — tightening regulations on emissions, tailings, and water use create open-ended balance-sheet risk that grows with each legislative cycle.
Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

sector_tailwinds: Operating margins 29% above sector median — the quantitative trace of pricing power
38 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
ROIC sits in the top quartile of Basic Materials peers — the moat is wider than the neighbourhood
Minimal goodwill on the balance sheet — low impairment risk

sect: Its 38% operating margin runs 29pp above the Basic Materials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.92x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 3.1% of sector revenue and 8.9% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-3.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 221 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 58% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 6% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 19% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 35% and a beta of 0.88, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $232.2M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 44% in the 2020 crash, 32% in the 2022 bear market and 74% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $66.64 (margin of safety -19%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 11%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $54.19 to $83.30 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Basic Materials peers: P/E 20.6 vs 16.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 79% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 4.6% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 8.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 7 covering analysts target $78.86 on average, 1% below the price.
prof: ROIC of 26% clears the cost of capital of 8.7% by 17pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.48).
It converts 18% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.68x.
ROE of 23% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.3x equity multiplier).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.4x net debt to EBITDA ($12.5B of cash against $21.5B of debt), with interest covered 11.0x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -7.7% over 3 years and 3.6% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 17%).
At current returns, reinvesting 9% of profits supports about 2.2% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 1.1% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Analysts expect 1.5% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.0%), and institutions hold 5%.
It returns 4.0% a year to shareholders (5.0% in dividends).
The share count has grown 11.5% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 38 consecutive years.
people: With about 38,833 employees, each generates about $1.3M of revenue, 2.1x the Basic Materials median, and revenue has grown 2.3% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $239K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.0M (2x revenue per employee).
